rx.title: Tretinoin and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: Using a Korean routine while you are on tretinoin
rx.qa: The usual advice is to let prescription tretinoin be the only strong active in the routine and let everything else do hydration, comfort and sun protection. In practice that means the dull half of a Korean shelf survives — a low-foam cleanser, a plain hydrating toner or essence, a calming moisturiser, sunscreen every morning — and the acids, scrubs and high-strength vitamin C go into a drawer. Whether you buffer, alternate or change anything at all is a question for the clinician who prescribed it, not for an article.

sections.h: Why tretinoin usually gets the night to itself
sections.body: Tretinoin is a prescription retinoid rather than a cosmetic retinol, and it does not need assistance. The early phase most people describe — tightness, flaking, rough patches beside the nose and mouth — gets worse when anything else exfoliates or stings. That is why routines shrink around it instead of growing. AHAs, BHAs, low-pH vitamin C, grain scrubs and the 각질 (gakjil, 'dead skin') removing gels sold everywhere in Korea are the first things people are commonly asked to set aside. If you want to keep one, raise it at your appointment rather than deciding by feel.

sections.h: What the Korean half of the routine is actually for
sections.body: What survives is the hydration and 진정 (jinjeong, 'calming') side: a watery toner or essence pressed in, a panthenol- or centella-leaning cream, a fragrance-free balm for the dry corners. None of this makes a prescription work better, and the popular line that hydrating layers 'boost penetration' is not something to bank on. What they do is make skin feel liveable while it adjusts, and comfort is not a trivial goal here. The most common reason a retinoid course goes nowhere is that the person stopped using it.

sections.h: The layering rules people repeat, and who should answer them
sections.body: Moisturiser first as a buffer. Alternating nights. Dry skin rather than damp. Leaving a gap after cleansing. All of these circulate as fixed rules, and all of them are really just levers for how much irritation a given person gets. Some prescribers suggest them, some do not, and the evidence separating them is thinner than the confidence with which they are repeated. Bring the question to the person who knows your skin, your climate and the rest of your shelf. A comment section knows none of those things.

sections.h: The part nobody gets to skip
sections.body: Sunscreen, every morning, reapplied when you are out. Retinoid-treated skin is commonly described as more sun-sensitive, tretinoin itself is degraded by UV, and unprotected exposure works against whatever change in tone or texture you were hoping for. This is where Korean formulation genuinely helps: the local sunscreen category is built around light fluids and gels that sit tolerably on flaking skin, where a thick cream can feel impossible. Pick the one you will actually reapply rather than the highest number on the tube.

rx.title: Adapalene and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: Adapalene alongside Korean skincare: what usually changes
rx.qa: Adapalene is the retinoid most people meet first — available without prescription in some countries and only with one in others — and it is generally treated as the more photostable, somewhat better-tolerated member of the family. The routine advice around it mirrors tretinoin's: no other exfoliating actives, generous hydration, sunscreen daily. Because availability and the right way to use it differ by country, the pharmacist or clinician who supplied yours is the one to ask, not a video.

sections.h: How it behaves differently
sections.body: Adapalene binds more selectively than older retinoids and is reported to be better tolerated at comparable use, though 'better tolerated' still means many people get a dry, tight, peeling stretch. Two practical differences matter. It is more stable in light, and it is stable alongside benzoyl peroxide, where tretinoin is classically broken down by it — which is why fixed combination products pair adapalene with peroxide rather than tretinoin. In Korea it generally comes through a clinic or pharmacy rather than off a cosmetics shelf, so it is not something to add casually on a trip.

sections.h: What comes out of the routine
sections.body: The same list as any prescription retinoid: acid toners, peeling pads, enzyme powders, scrub cleansers, cleansing brushes and the strong low-pH vitamin C serums that already sting on a good day. Korean routines make this harder than it sounds, because exfoliation is often built into products that do not look like exfoliants — 필링 (piling) pads sold as a toner step, gommage sticks, 'texture refining' essences. Read the ingredient list rather than the marketing line, and if you are unsure, put it aside until you can ask.

sections.h: What is worth keeping
sections.body: A gentle cleanser that does not leave skin squeaking, a simple hydrating layer, a moisturiser weighted towards ceramides, panthenol or centella, and sunscreen. Korea's strength here is texture: light gel creams for oily skin that still want comfort, and thicker 크림 (keurim) or balm textures for the flaking phase. Fragrance is the thing to watch — a great many otherwise sensible Korean moisturisers are scented, and that is exactly what most clinicians would rather you avoid while skin is reacting.

sections.h: Purging, patience and honest expectations
sections.body: An early flare gets called purging and the term does real work for some people and cover for others. A retinoid speeding up what was already forming under the surface is plausible; a rash, swelling, weeping or spreading irritation is not purging and is worth reporting. Nobody can tell you from a distance which one you have. What is reasonably clear is that retinoids reward consistency over intensity, and that stopping and restarting repeatedly produces the irritation without the payoff. Your prescriber decides what to do if the reaction is not settling.

rx.title: Tazarotene and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: Tazarotene: the strictest retinoid to build a routine around
rx.qa: Tazarotene is prescription-only and generally considered the most irritating of the common topical retinoids, so the routine around it is usually stripped further back than it would be for tretinoin or adapalene. Expect a clinician to want a bland cleanser, a plain moisturiser and daily sunscreen, and to want everything that exfoliates, tingles or fragrances removed. Every decision about how and when it is applied belongs to the prescriber, including any decision to change it.

sections.h: Why the routine gets smaller than usual
sections.body: The stronger the retinoid, the less room there is for anything else, and tazarotene sits at the demanding end. Dryness, stinging on application, visible peeling and a temporarily rough surface are commonly reported, which means the supporting products have one job: keep the skin comfortable enough that you continue. This is not the moment for a ten-step routine, a new essence you saw recommended, or a 각질 (gakjil) removing gel. If a product does anything other than cleanse, hydrate, moisturise or block UV, assume it is out until you have asked.

sections.h: Sensation is not a progress meter
sections.body: A persistent belief in beauty forums is that a strong reaction means it is working. It does not follow. Irritation and the changes a retinoid is prescribed for are not the same process, and a face too sore to keep treating has stopped delivering anything at all. Korean skincare is unusually well equipped for the comfort side — 저자극 (jeojageuk, 'low-irritation') lines, unscented barrier creams, thick sleeping masks used simply as an overnight occlusive. Use them for that, and let the prescriber judge whether the reaction you are having is within the expected range.

sections.h: Pregnancy, planning and the conversation to have early
sections.body: Topical retinoids as a class are treated cautiously in pregnancy, and tazarotene is handled with particular strictness by prescribers. This is not a decision to work out from an article or a forum thread. If you are pregnant, trying to conceive or considering it, that belongs at the top of the conversation with the clinician who prescribed it and with whoever manages your pregnancy care — before anything changes, not after. The same applies to anyone else's prescription: it is theirs, and sharing it is a genuinely bad idea.

sections.h: Sun protection carries more weight here
sections.body: Skin treated with a strong retinoid is commonly described as more sun-sensitive, and the surface is often flaking, which makes an even sunscreen layer harder to achieve. Korean sun fluids and light gels tend to sit better over flaking than heavy creams, and a hat plus shade does work no formula can. Reapplication over a dry, patchy surface is the practical problem people underestimate — a cushion or stick over a fluid is one common workaround, and the honest answer is that it protects less well than a fresh full layer.

rx.title: Oral Isotretinoin and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: What a Korean routine looks like during oral isotretinoin
rx.qa: During an oral isotretinoin course the routine almost always simplifies to a mild cleanser, a rich fragrance-free moisturiser, an ointment for lips and sunscreen, with actives and exfoliants set aside. Skin is commonly described as drier, more fragile and more easily irritated than usual, and the same is true of lips, eyes and the inside of the nose. This is a prescribed medication with monitoring attached, so anything about the course itself — including starting, pausing or stopping — is entirely for the prescribing clinician.

sections.h: Everything the routine was doing before is now the medication's job
sections.body: The oil-control toner, the BHA, the clay mask, the acne spot gel: on an isotretinoin course most of these become redundant at best and abrasive at worst. Oiliness usually falls sharply, and continuing to fight it strips a surface that is already struggling. Korean routines built around 모공 (mogong, 'pores') and mattifying tend to age badly here. What people are commonly advised to keep is short and boring, and the boringness is the point — fewer variables while skin is behaving unusually, and fewer things to blame if something flares.

sections.h: The parts of you nobody warns about
sections.body: Lips are the near-universal complaint, and a plain occlusive ointment used often beats any tinted balm. Dryness inside the nose, dry or gritty eyes, and skin on hands, arms and shins that cracks in cold air are all commonly reported. Contact lens wearers often find their lenses less comfortable. None of this is fixed by facial skincare, so extend the thinking: an unscented body cream, an ointment by the bed, humidity indoors in a Korean winter. Anything that is painful, worsening or affecting your vision goes to your doctor, not a shopping list.

sections.h: Procedures, waxing and the timing question
sections.body: Skin is commonly described as more fragile during and after a course, and clinics routinely ask about isotretinoin before waxing, peels, laser and other treatments. The long-standing blanket caution around resurfacing has been re-examined by specialists in recent years and expert opinion has softened for some procedures, but that is precisely the judgement that belongs to the doctor holding the device — not to you, and not to a beauty therapist working from a form. Declare it, in writing, every time, including for eyebrow threading and salon facials where people forget to mention it.

sections.h: What Korean products still earn a place
sections.body: Thick unscented creams, 판테놀 (panteneol, panthenol) and ceramide-led barrier products, cream cleansers that rinse without squeaking, and sleeping packs used purely as an overnight occlusive. Sheet masks are a mixed case: the fabric is harmless, but many essences carry alcohol, fragrance or extracts that sting on compromised skin, and a stinging mask is telling you something. Sunscreen stays, and photosensitivity is commonly flagged during a course. Anything labelled brightening, peeling, resurfacing or tingling can wait until the prescriber says otherwise.

rx.title: Benzoyl Peroxide and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: Benzoyl peroxide beside Korean skincare: what it wrecks, what it needs
rx.qa: Benzoyl peroxide is drying, it bleaches fabric and hair, and it does not sit politely with every other product — which is why routines built around it are usually simplified and kept fragrance-free. Most people are advised to pair it with generous moisturising rather than more actives, and to be careful about what it touches. Whether you use it at all, and alongside what, is a decision for the clinician or pharmacist who recommended it.

sections.h: The laundry problem is real, and it is permanent
sections.body: Benzoyl peroxide bleaches cotton. Towels, pillowcases, flannel headbands, the collar of a favourite shirt, and hair if a leave-on product migrates overnight. There is no fixing the marks afterwards. White bedding and white towels are the standard workaround, along with letting it dry properly before anything touches your face. This sounds trivial next to the skincare questions and it is the single thing people are most annoyed about missing. It also applies to a partner's pillowcase, which is a conversation worth having in advance.

sections.h: What it does and does not combine with
sections.body: Benzoyl peroxide is an oxidiser, and it is classically described as degrading tretinoin when the two are applied together, while adapalene is stable alongside it — which is why fixed combinations pair peroxide with adapalene. The same oxidising nature is why people are often told to keep it away from a pure vitamin C serum in the same layer. Clinicians commonly prescribe it with a topical antibiotic specifically to reduce the chance of bacterial resistance developing. How any of these are sequenced across a day is a prescription question, not a preference.

sections.h: The storage point worth knowing
sections.body: There has been an ongoing regulatory conversation about benzene forming in benzoyl peroxide products, particularly when they are stored warm, and it has produced recalls in some markets. The sensible domestic response is unglamorous: keep the tube cool, do not leave it in a car in a Korean August, do not stockpile it on a sunny windowsill, and check expiry. Where that conversation currently stands is something a pharmacist can tell you more reliably than a search result, and it is a fair question to ask when you collect it.

sections.h: The Korean products that pair sensibly
sections.body: Comfort products, essentially. A cream cleanser or low-foam gel rather than a squeaky high-pH foam, a plain hydrating toner, and a moisturiser leaning on ceramides, 판테놀 (panteneol, panthenol) or centella. Korea's 진정 (jinjeong, 'calming') category is genuinely useful alongside a drying prescription — provided you pick the fragrance-free, alcohol-light versions rather than the ones that tingle. What does not pair sensibly is another acne active bought on top. Two drying products is not twice the result, it is twice the irritation, and it is how people end up stopping.

rx.title: Topical Acne Antibiotics and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: Topical antibiotics for acne: how the rest of the routine adjusts
rx.qa: Topical antibiotics for acne are usually prescribed alongside something else — commonly benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid — rather than on their own, because using them alone is associated with bacterial resistance. The routine around them is generally kept simple and non-irritating, since some formulations are alcohol-based and drying. Which combination you are on, and for how long, is entirely the prescriber's call.

sections.h: Why they are rarely prescribed alone
sections.body: Antibiotic resistance is the reason, and it is not a theoretical concern in acne care. Clinicians commonly pair a topical antibiotic with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid, often as a single combination product, because the pairing is associated with less resistance developing than the antibiotic used by itself. That matters for you in a practical way: if a prescription came as two products, using only the one that stings less defeats the design. If the combination is uncomfortable, say so at your appointment rather than quietly editing it.

sections.h: The formulations differ more than the names suggest
sections.body: The same active can arrive as a gel, a lotion, a foam or an alcohol-based solution, and they do not feel alike. Alcohol-based solutions dry quickly and can leave skin tight, which pushes people towards heavier moisturising than they expected. Others are bland enough that the routine barely changes. Read what you were actually given, and if the texture is the problem rather than the medication, that is a genuinely useful thing to report — prescribers can often switch the vehicle without changing the plan.

sections.h: What a Korean routine contributes
sections.body: Hydration and barrier comfort, and not much else. A gentle cleanser, a watery toner or essence, and a moisturiser weighted towards ceramides or centella will do more for adherence than any additional acne product bought in Myeongdong. What is worth resisting is the Korean acne shelf itself: tea tree spot gels, sulphur masks, salicylic pads and 모공 (mogong, 'pore') toners stacked on top of a prescription is how a manageable routine becomes a raw one. One acne plan at a time.

sections.h: Sun, staining and the practical notes
sections.body: Any benzoyl peroxide in the combination bleaches fabric, so white towels and pillowcases apply here too. Sunscreen stays, both because a retinoid may be part of the same plan and because post-blemish marks look worse with unprotected exposure. Korea's light sun fluids make daily use realistic on oily, medicated skin where a thick cream would not survive the commute. Anything that looks like an allergic reaction — spreading redness, swelling, hives, worsening rather than settling — is a call to the prescriber, not a reason to add a soothing mask.

rx.title: Oral Acne Antibiotics and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: On oral antibiotics for acne: what changes in the routine
rx.qa: Oral antibiotics for acne are generally prescribed as a time-limited part of a wider plan, almost always with a topical treatment alongside, and the tetracycline family commonly used carries a well-known caution about sun sensitivity. The skincare adjustments are therefore mostly about sun protection and keeping the topical routine gentle enough to continue. Course length, choice and any change to it are decisions for the prescribing clinician alone.

sections.h: Sun sensitivity is the headline
sections.body: Several oral antibiotics used for acne — the tetracyclines in particular — are commonly flagged for photosensitivity, meaning skin can react to sun exposure more readily than usual. This is not a reason to panic and it is a reason to take shade, clothing and sunscreen seriously rather than performatively. If your plan involves a summer in Korea, a beach holiday or long days outdoors, mention it before the prescription is written. Ask your own prescriber whether the specific one you are on carries this caution, because they do not all behave the same way.

sections.h: They are usually part of a plan, not the plan
sections.body: Oral antibiotics are typically combined with a topical — benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid — rather than used alone, for the same resistance reasons that apply to topical antibiotics, and they are generally not intended as an indefinite arrangement. That has a practical consequence people miss: the topical part is what usually continues afterwards, so it is worth getting comfortable with it early. If the topical is the bit you have quietly abandoned because it stings, that is exactly what to raise at the follow-up.

sections.h: The rest of the body, and the rest of you
sections.body: Oral treatment reaches everywhere, and stomach upset, thrush and general digestive grumbling are commonly reported with antibiotics as a class. There is a persistent online enthusiasm for probiotics as the answer; the evidence is mixed rather than settled, and it is a question for a pharmacist or doctor who knows what you are taking. Interactions with other medications, supplements and even how you take it relative to food can matter. Read the leaflet you were given, then ask about anything on it you do not understand.

sections.h: What the Korean routine should be doing
sections.body: Staying calm and staying on. A gentle cleanser, hydration, a fragrance-light moisturiser and a sunscreen you will reapply. Korea's sun fluids and cushions make midday reapplication realistic, which matters more than usual here. The temptation while waiting for results is to keep adding — a 진정 (jinjeong, 'calming') ampoule, a peeling pad, a new spot treatment — and each addition makes it harder to tell what is working. Change one thing at a time, and let the appointment, not the mirror at 11pm, decide whether the plan is working.

rx.title: Prescription Azelaic Acid and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: Prescription-strength azelaic acid alongside Korean skincare
rx.qa: Prescription azelaic acid is a different proposition from the cosmetic azelaic derivatives sold in serums, and it is commonly reported to tingle, itch or sting for a while after application. The routine around it is usually kept simple, fragrance-free and free of additional acids, with sunscreen daily. It is prescribed for specific reasons in specific situations, so what it is doing for you and how it fits your day is a conversation with your clinician.

sections.h: Prescription strength is not the same as the serum
sections.body: Cosmetic products often use azelaic derivatives such as potassium azeloyl diglycinate, or azelaic acid at cosmetic levels, and they behave differently from what a prescriber dispenses. Comparing the two by name alone is misleading. Korea's cosmetics rules do not treat azelaic acid as one of the 기능성화장품 (gineungseong hwajangpum, 'functional cosmetics') brightening actives, so a Korean shelf will more often offer niacinamide, arbutin or tranexamic-type ingredients instead. If you want an azelaic product for cosmetic use, that is a separate decision from the prescription.

sections.h: The tingling is common and it still deserves a mention
sections.body: Transient stinging, itching, warmth and a flush after application are commonly reported and often described as easing with continued use. That does not mean every reaction is fine. Worsening burning, swelling or a rash that spreads is worth reporting rather than absorbing. Because a tingle is expected, people stack other tingling products on top and lose the ability to tell which one is responsible — an acid toner, a strong vitamin C, a warming cleanser. Keep the rest of the routine boring so the signal stays readable.

sections.h: Redness, pigmentation and honest expectations
sections.body: Azelaic acid is prescribed in contexts involving both blemishes and uneven tone, and it is one of the options clinicians reach for when others are ruled out for a particular person. What it will do for your face specifically is not something an article can promise, and results in this territory are generally gradual rather than dramatic. Expect the appearance of tone to shift slowly if at all, expect sun exposure to work against it, and let the person who prescribed it set the expectation.

sections.h: What to layer, and what to hold back
sections.body: A mild cleanser, a hydrating layer, a fragrance-free moisturiser and daily sunscreen cover it. Korean 진정 (jinjeong, 'calming') creams built on centella or madecassoside pair sensibly, and light gel textures suit skin that is already flushing. Hold back on AHAs, BHAs, scrubs, strong vitamin C and anything marketed as resurfacing while you settle in. If you want to reintroduce one later, do it one product at a time and tell your prescriber what you have added — including the ones you assume are too gentle to matter.

rx.title: Hydroquinone and a Korean Brightening Routine
rx.h1: Hydroquinone and the Korean brightening shelf: two different worlds
rx.qa: Hydroquinone is not permitted in cosmetics in Korea, the EU or Japan, and in the United States it is no longer sold over the counter — where it is used, it comes through a clinician who manages the course. That matters because Korea's brightening category is built entirely on other actives, so a Korean routine is a companion to a hydroquinone plan, never a substitute for one. Everything about strength, duration and breaks belongs to the prescriber.

sections.h: Why you will not find it on a Korean shelf
sections.body: Korea regulates brightening claims through the 기능성화장품 (gineungseong hwajangpum, 'functional cosmetics') system, and the approved 미백 (mibaek, 'brightening') actives are a defined list — niacinamide and arbutin among the familiar ones. Hydroquinone is not on it. Anything sold to you as a Korean cream containing hydroquinone is either mislabelled or not a cosmetic, and creams bought informally overseas have repeatedly turned out to contain undeclared ingredients. If a clinic in Korea dispenses something for pigmentation, it is dispensing it as a clinic, with a consultation attached.

sections.h: Why courses are managed rather than open-ended
sections.body: Prescribers generally treat hydroquinone as something used in a planned way rather than indefinitely, partly because of irritation and partly because of exogenous ochronosis, an uncommon but reported darkening associated with prolonged use. That is precisely why it is not a shelf product. Anyone offering you an unlimited supply without follow-up is doing you no favours. If a pigmentation plan involves it, the review appointments are part of the plan, not an optional extra, and any decision to continue, pause or switch is the clinician's.

sections.h: What the Korean routine can genuinely add
sections.body: Sunscreen, relentlessly, because unprotected UV works against every pigmentation approach that exists — and Korea's sunscreen category is the most usable in the world, which makes daily reapplication realistic instead of aspirational. Beyond that: niacinamide, arbutin, tranexamic-type ingredients and vitamin C are the cosmetic supporting cast, and they are cosmetic. They influence the look of tone gradually. Whether any of them belong on top of a prescription, and in what order, is worth asking rather than assuming, because irritation on treated skin can leave marks of its own.

sections.h: The melasma reality check
sections.body: If the pigmentation in question is melasma, temper the marketing. It is widely described as recurring, sun- and heat-sensitive, and stubborn even under specialist care, and no Korean essence changes that. Heat matters as well as light — a 찜질방 (jjimjilbang, Korean bathhouse) session, a hot yoga class or a steaming commute can undo careful work. The realistic frame is long-term management by a clinician with cosmetic support around it, not a course of anything that finishes. Anyone promising to clear it permanently is selling something.

rx.title: Topical Steroids and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: Topical steroids: what the rest of the routine should and should not do
rx.qa: Topical corticosteroids come in a range of potencies and are prescribed for defined situations and defined areas, with facial use handled especially carefully — none of which is something to work out from an article. Around them, the usual advice is a bland fragrance-free routine and a plain moisturiser, with actives paused while skin is flaring. How much, where and for how long is entirely the prescriber's territory, including any decision to stop.

sections.h: Potency, site and why the label matters
sections.body: Steroid creams are not interchangeable. Potency classes differ substantially, and clinicians choose differently for the face, the eyelids, body folds and thicker skin elsewhere, because absorption differs by site. A tube prescribed for a patch on someone's elbow is not automatically appropriate for a cheek. This is the most common informal-sharing error in skincare, and it is worth stating plainly: use what was prescribed to you, where it was prescribed for, and take leftover tubes back to a pharmacy rather than improvising with them later.

sections.h: The unlabelled cream problem
sections.body: Regulators in a number of countries have issued warnings about creams sold online and informally that were found to contain undeclared corticosteroids, often marketed for eczema, brightening or 'miracle' calming. The pattern is recognisable: dramatic early results, no ingredient list you can verify, no manufacturer you can trace, sold through social media. Korea's cosmetics rules require a full 전성분 (jeonseongbun, 'full ingredient list') on the packaging, so a product without one is already outside the system. If a cream works far too well and nobody can tell you why, be suspicious.

sections.h: Steroid withdrawal, honestly
sections.body: Topical steroid withdrawal is discussed intensely online and the discussion outruns the evidence. Some clinicians recognise a withdrawal pattern after prolonged potent use; others dispute how common it is and how it should be defined, and the published evidence is genuinely thin in both directions. What follows from that uncertainty is not self-tapering based on forum protocols, which is how flares get worse and skin infections get missed. If you are worried about how long you have been using something, that worry is a reason to book an appointment.

sections.h: What Korean skincare does alongside
sections.body: Moisturising, and staying out of the way. A non-foaming or low-foam cleanser, an unscented cream or ointment, and generous, frequent application are the standard supporting advice for inflamed skin. Korea's 저자극 (jeojageuk, 'low-irritation') and derma lines suit this well, provided you check for fragrance, which many otherwise gentle Korean products still carry. Sheet masks, acid toners, vitamin C and exfoliants generally wait. Sunscreen still matters, and a mineral-leaning formula is often more comfortable on skin that stings. Ask your prescriber how a moisturiser should be timed relative to the steroid.

rx.title: Calcineurin Inhibitors and a Korean Routine
rx.h1: Tacrolimus, pimecrolimus and the routine built around them
rx.qa: Topical calcineurin inhibitors are prescribed as a steroid-sparing option in some situations, commonly for delicate areas such as the face and eyelids, and a burning or stinging sensation on application is frequently reported early on. The supporting routine is the usual bland one — gentle cleansing, a fragrance-free moisturiser, daily sun protection — with actives paused. What they are for, where they go and how long they continue is decided by the prescribing clinician.

sections.h: Why clinicians reach for them
sections.body: They are used partly because they do not carry the skin-thinning concerns associated with prolonged potent steroid use, which makes them attractive for eyelids, around the mouth and other thin-skinned areas where steroids are handled cautiously. They also carry a warning label about a theoretical long-term risk that has been debated for years and is not settled in the way the label's prominence suggests. That debate belongs in the consulting room. What it means for you practically is that this is a prescription with a conversation attached, and the conversation is worth having properly.

sections.h: The stinging, and what makes it worse
sections.body: A burning, warm or stinging sensation shortly after application is commonly reported and often described as easing with continued use. Several things reliably make it worse: applying to skin that is already raw, applying immediately after a hot shower, and — with tacrolimus specifically — alcohol, where a flushing reaction has been reported. In Korea that last one has a social dimension worth planning for around 회식 (hoesik, work dinners). If the sensation is severe or not settling, that is information for your prescriber rather than a problem to solve with a cooling mask.

sections.h: Sun protection is part of the plan
sections.body: Sun protection is routinely emphasised with these medications, and it is one of the areas where a Korean routine genuinely earns its place. The local sunscreen category is unusually good at light textures and mineral options that do not sting, which matters when the treated area is an eyelid or a raw patch beside the nose. Hats, sunglasses and shade do work that no formula matches. Ask your prescriber how sunscreen and the medication should be sequenced, because the answer depends on the product and the area.

sections.h: What to keep and what to shelve
sections.body: Keep a mild cleanser, a plain unscented moisturiser used generously, and sun protection. Shelve acids, retinoids, strong vitamin C, scrubs and anything that tingles, at least while things are active. Korea's 진정 (jinjeong, 'calming') category overlaps neatly with what is wanted here — centella, madecassoside, panthenol, heartleaf — but read for fragrance and alcohol, and be wary of adding a brand-new product to skin that is already reacting. One change at a time, reported at your next appointment.

rx.title: Hormonal Acne Treatment and Your Skincare
rx.h1: When acne is managed hormonally: how the routine shifts
rx.qa: Some persistent acne is managed with oral medication that works hormonally rather than on the skin surface, and where that route is appropriate is a clinical judgement involving your history, other medications and monitoring — not something a skincare article can weigh in on. What the routine tends to look like is simpler: less oil control, more comfort, and patience, because these approaches are generally described as gradual. Everything about whether, what and how long belongs to the prescribing clinician.

sections.h: What 'hormonal' means here, and what it does not
sections.body: Dermatologists sometimes discuss oral options — spironolactone and combined hormonal contraception are the ones most often mentioned — for acne patterns that look hormonally driven, typically along the jaw and lower face and often cycling with the month. Whether any of them is appropriate depends on medical history, other medications, monitoring and personal circumstances, and the answer is genuinely different from person to person. It is worth knowing these routes exist so you can ask about them. It is not worth deciding in advance which one you want.

sections.h: Your skin may behave differently than it used to
sections.body: If oil production drops, a routine built for oily skin stops fitting. Mattifying toners, clay masks, foaming cleansers chosen for their squeak and 모공 (mogong, 'pore') products can start to feel harsh on skin that no longer needs managing that way. The common mistake is not noticing for months. Reassess textures rather than adding products: a cream cleanser instead of a gel, a richer moisturiser in winter, fewer oil-control steps. Korea's enormous range of moisturiser weights is genuinely useful for this kind of gradual recalibration.

sections.h: Timelines, monitoring and the trap of judging early
sections.body: Approaches in this territory are generally described as slow, which means the mirror is a poor guide in the short term and the appointment is a better one. Some plans involve blood tests or other monitoring, and those appointments are part of the treatment rather than admin. The trap is changing your skincare every few weeks in response to normal fluctuation, then being unable to tell what did what. Keep the routine stable, keep dated photos in the same light if you find that useful, and let the clinician interpret.

sections.h: What the Korean routine contributes
sections.body: Cosmetic support and nothing more: gentle cleansing, hydration, a fragrance-light moisturiser, sunscreen, and — if your clinician agrees — something for the appearance of post-blemish marks such as niacinamide or a tranexamic-type ingredient. Post-inflammatory marks fade slowly and unprotected sun makes them worse, so sunscreen is doing more of the work here than any brightening serum. Resist the urge to run an aggressive acne routine alongside an oral plan. Two treatments competing on one face makes irritation likely and attribution impossible.

rx.title: Oral Antihistamines and Your Skincare
rx.h1: Taking an antihistamine for itchy skin: what skincare can and cannot do
rx.qa: Oral antihistamines are commonly used where itching is driven by histamine — hives being the clearest case — and are generally described as less useful for the itch of dry or eczema-prone skin, where moisturising does more. Drowsiness with the older sedating types and a general dryness of skin, eyes and mouth are commonly reported. Which type suits you, and whether an antihistamine is the right tool at all, is a question for a pharmacist or doctor.

sections.h: Not all itch is the same itch
sections.body: Histamine drives the itch of hives, and antihistamines are used accordingly. The itch of dry, cracked or eczema-prone skin is usually described as driven by other mechanisms, which is why people take an antihistamine for it and report that it did very little beyond making them sleepy. That is useful information rather than a failure of the medicine. If itching is persistent, spreading, keeping you awake or accompanied by swelling or breathing changes, that is a medical conversation and, in the case of breathing, an urgent one.

sections.h: The dryness that comes with them
sections.body: Antihistamines are commonly associated with a general drying effect — dry mouth, dry or gritty eyes, and skin that feels less comfortable than usual. That interacts badly with a Korean winter, an over-air-conditioned office and a routine full of foaming cleansers. The practical response is unremarkable: a milder cleanser, a heavier moisturiser, humidity indoors, and eye drops if the eyes are the problem. Contact lens wearers often notice it first. Report anything persistent rather than layering more products over it.

sections.h: What Korean skincare actually helps with
sections.body: Barrier comfort. A cream cleanser or low-foam gel, a hydrating 수분 (subun, 'moisture') layer, a fragrance-free cream weighted towards ceramides, panthenol or centella, and generous application at the moment skin is still slightly damp. On itchy skin, cool matters more than warm: lukewarm showers, a moisturiser stored in the fridge if you like. Skip the tingling essences and the acid toners entirely while things are irritable. Nothing cosmetic addresses hives; it makes the surrounding skin more comfortable, which is a real but limited job.

sections.h: Scratching, sleep and the honest limits
sections.body: Broken skin from scratching is a genuine risk and it is worse at night, which is part of why sedating antihistamines are sometimes discussed for evening use — a decision for a clinician, not a self-experiment. Short nails, cotton gloves and cool bedding do more than most people expect. Be sceptical of Korean products marketed for itch relief with vague soothing language; the category is largely cosmetic. If the itch has a cause nobody has identified yet, finding it matters more than what you put on top.

rx.title: Before and After a Chemical Peel
rx.h1: Peels: what usually comes out of the routine, and when it returns
rx.qa: Before a peel, clinics commonly ask patients to pause retinoids, acids, scrubs and anything that has recently irritated the skin, and to declare every prescription and recent procedure. Afterwards the routine typically shrinks to a bland cleanser, a plain moisturiser and sun protection until the clinic says otherwise. The only timeline that counts is the written one your clinic gives you, and it varies by peel, by depth and by person.

sections.h: What the pre-appointment questions are actually for
sections.body: The form asking about retinoids, recent waxing, cold sores, isotretinoin and recent sun exposure is not bureaucracy. Skin that has been exfoliated, waxed, burnt or medicated behaves differently under an acid, and a peel applied to unexpectedly thin skin is where problems come from. Declare everything, including products you think are too gentle to count, brow threading, a facial last week and any prescription from a different doctor. Bring the actual bottles or photographs of the ingredient lists if you are unsure what is in them.

sections.h: The gap between a clinic peel and a home one
sections.body: Korean shelves are full of 필링 (piling) products — pads, gels, powders, gommage sticks — and they operate in a different league from a clinic 시술 (siseul, 'procedure'). The risk is not that the home version does too much; it is that people keep using it during the run-up to an appointment without registering it as exfoliation, because it is sold as a toner or a mask. Read the ingredient list for acids and enzymes rather than the front of the packet, and mention anything you have been using.

sections.h: Afterwards: fewer products, not better ones
sections.body: The standard aftercare pattern is bland cleansing, a simple moisturiser without actives or fragrance, and sun protection once the clinic confirms the skin surface tolerates it. This is the moment people most want to help things along with a new 진정 (jinjeong, 'calming') ampoule, and it is the worst moment to introduce an unfamiliar product. Peeling that appears should be left to come away on its own; picking or scrubbing it is how marks form. Heat is the underrated variable — saunas, 찜질방 (jjimjilbang), hot showers and hard exercise are commonly postponed.

sections.h: When to call rather than search
sections.body: Pain that increases rather than eases, spreading redness or warmth, blistering, discharge or fever are reasons to contact the clinic promptly. Do not wait to see whether a forum agrees. Visitors to Korea should sort the follow-up question out before booking: who covers complications, how to reach them, and what happens once you have flown home, at which point a licensed doctor where you live becomes the person to call. Ask what the clinic expects normal recovery to look like, so you can recognise when it is not.

rx.title: Before and After a Laser Appointment
rx.h1: Laser appointments: what the routine pauses, and what it must not skip
rx.qa: Before laser work, clinics commonly ask patients to avoid tanning and sun exposure, pause exfoliating actives and retinoids, and declare medications — oral isotretinoin and photosensitising drugs in particular. Afterwards the routine usually reduces to gentle cleansing, a plain moisturiser and strict sun protection for as long as the clinic specifies. Every one of those decisions is device-, setting- and person-specific, so the clinic's written instructions override anything written here.

sections.h: A tan changes the calculation
sections.body: Many lasers work by targeting pigment, which means recent sun exposure or a tan alters how the treatment behaves and raises the risk of unwanted pigment changes afterwards. This is why clinics ask about sun and why the honest answer matters more than the convenient one. It also makes the run-up to an appointment a poor time for a beach weekend, and it makes the weeks after one a poor time too. Sunscreen before and after is not a suggestion here; it is part of the procedure.

sections.h: The medication questions
sections.body: Photosensitising medications — some antibiotics among them — and a history of oral isotretinoin are standard items on a consent form for good reasons. The long-standing blanket caution about resurfacing after isotretinoin has been re-examined by specialists in recent years and expert opinion has softened for some procedures, but that judgement belongs to the doctor operating the device. Declare it either way. A history of cold sores is another common question, because some treatments are associated with triggering an outbreak and clinicians sometimes plan for that in advance.

sections.h: Afterwards, the routine gets boring on purpose
sections.body: Gentle cleansing, a plain moisturiser without actives or fragrance, and sun protection once the clinic confirms the surface tolerates it. Any crusting or flaking is left alone. Heat is a recurring theme in Korean aftercare specifically — 찜질방 (jjimjilbang), saunas, hot springs, steamy showers and hard training all raise skin temperature and blood flow, and clinics routinely ask patients to postpone them. If your Korea itinerary is built around a bathhouse day, mention it before booking rather than after, because the sequencing usually cannot be fixed retrospectively.

sections.h: Expectations, sold and real
sections.body: Korean clinics market 레이저 토닝 (leijeo toning, 'laser toning') and similar treatments as course-based, and course-based is generally accurate — single-session transformation is a marketing frame rather than a typical outcome. Ask what result is realistic for your skin and what the clinic does if it does not materialise. Ask about pigment risks for your skin tone specifically, because responses differ. Increasing pain, spreading redness, blistering or discharge afterwards means contacting the clinic promptly rather than waiting to see.

rx.title: Before and After Microneedling
rx.h1: Microneedling: the aftercare question is really a product question
rx.qa: Microneedling temporarily makes the skin surface far more permeable, which turns the ordinary question of what to apply into a safety question — clinics commonly restrict aftercare to what they supply or specify. Beforehand the usual instruction is to pause retinoids, acids and scrubs and to declare medications and recent procedures. Depth, device, settings and recovery all vary, so the clinic's written aftercare governs, not a routine you found online.

sections.h: Permeability is the whole point and the whole risk
sections.body: The reason people are told not to apply their usual serum afterwards is that ingredients formulated to sit on intact skin may reach places they were never tested for. Reactions to substances applied onto freshly needled skin have been reported, including with vitamin C serums, which is precisely the product people assume is helpful. Preservatives, fragrance and botanical extracts all belong to the same category of concern. If the clinic supplies or specifies what goes on afterwards, use that and nothing else until they say otherwise.

sections.h: Home rollers deserve more scepticism than they get
sections.body: Home devices are sold widely in Korea and elsewhere, and the honest position is that they are a different proposition from a clinic device — different needle length, different control, and a sterility problem that is entirely on you. Cleaning a roller properly between uses is harder than it looks, and a used one is not something to share, ever. Rolling over active blemishes is a well-known way to spread them. If you use one at all, treat it as a device with real risks rather than a skincare step.

sections.h: Before the appointment
sections.body: The standard pre-treatment pattern is to pause retinoids, AHAs, BHAs, scrubs and anything that has recently irritated the skin, and to declare oral medications, recent procedures, a history of cold sores and any tendency to keloid scarring. Korean 각질 (gakjil, 'exfoliating') products are easy to forget on a form because they are often sold as toners or masks. Arrive with clean skin and no makeup if the clinic asks for that, and be honest about a sunburn even if it means rebooking.

sections.h: Afterwards, and when to call
sections.body: Expect the clinic to specify a very short routine and to ask you to avoid makeup, sun, heat and exercise for a defined period that is theirs to set. Do not add a sheet mask because your skin feels dry, do not exfoliate the flaking, and do not restart actives on your own schedule. Increasing pain, spreading redness or warmth, pus, unusual swelling or fever means contacting the clinic promptly. If you were treated abroad and have flown home, a licensed doctor where you live is who you call.

rx.title: Before and After Injectables
rx.h1: Injectables: what to disclose, what to expect, what is an emergency
rx.qa: Around injectable treatments the important skincare adjustments are small and the important disclosures are large — tell the injector every medication and supplement you take and let them decide what matters, rather than pausing anything yourself. Afterwards clinics commonly restrict pressure, heat, exercise and makeup over injection points for a period they specify. Some complications are genuine emergencies, so knowing the warning signs before you book is part of preparing sensibly.

sections.h: Disclose, do not self-adjust
sections.body: Certain medications and supplements are widely discussed as making bruising more likely — blood thinners, some pain relievers, fish oil, ginkgo and others. The correct move is to list everything you take at the consultation and let the injector and, where relevant, your own doctor decide. Stopping a prescribed medication before a cosmetic appointment is not a decision to make yourself, and no article should be the reason you do. Bring an actual list rather than trying to remember, including anything taken occasionally.

sections.h: What the skincare side looks like
sections.body: Modest. Clinics commonly ask patients to keep injection points clean, avoid makeup over them for a specified period, and avoid pressing, massaging or lying face-down on the treated area — including during facials and massages, which people book without thinking. Heat is restricted for the same reasons it is after other procedures, so 찜질방 (jjimjilbang) visits, saunas and hard training are usually postponed. Actives generally pause briefly. Beyond that, your normal gentle routine and sunscreen resume when the clinic says so.

sections.h: The warning signs that mean act now
sections.body: Skin turning white, grey, mottled or dusky after a filler injection, pain out of proportion to what was expected, or any change in vision are reasons to contact the clinic immediately and seek urgent medical attention. These are recognised emergencies where time matters, and they are not something to research first. Know the clinic's out-of-hours contact before you are injected, not afterwards. Bruising, swelling and tenderness are common and different; anything that is worsening rather than settling still warrants a call.

sections.h: Questions worth asking before you book
sections.body: What exactly is being injected, under which name and by whom — Korean clinics offer a wide menu of injectable categories and the labels used in marketing are often looser than the labels used in medicine. Ask who performs the injection and what their qualification is. Ask what happens if there is a complication after you fly home, because the answer is often that you will be relying on a doctor where you live. A clinic that answers all of that plainly is a better sign than a discount.

rx.title: Sunscreen While You Are on a Retinoid
rx.h1: Sunscreen on retinoid-treated skin: the practical problems nobody mentions
rx.qa: Sunscreen is the one step that stays non-negotiable on any retinoid, prescription or cosmetic, because treated skin is commonly described as more sun-sensitive and unprotected exposure works against the reason you are using it. The real difficulty is practical rather than principled: flaking, tight skin makes an even layer and midday reapplication harder. Korean sunscreen textures help with exactly that, though your prescriber sets the rest of the plan.

sections.h: Why it matters more here than usual
sections.body: Retinoid-treated skin is routinely described as more sun-sensitive, and tretinoin itself is degraded by UV, which is part of why topical retinoids are typically applied at night. There is also a simpler argument. If you are using a retinoid for the look of tone, texture or fine lines, unprotected sun exposure is working directly against the outcome. Sunscreen is not a supporting act in this routine; it is the half of it that runs in daylight, and skipping it makes the other half largely decorative.

sections.h: The flaking problem, honestly
sections.body: Sunscreen applied over peeling skin goes on unevenly, catches on rough patches and pills under makeup, and no formula fully solves it. What helps is preparation rather than product-hopping: a hydrating layer underneath so the surface is not gripping, a moisturiser given a moment to settle, and application by patting rather than dragging. Some people find a mineral formula sits worse on flaking, others find the opposite. Reapplication over a patchy surface protects less well than a fresh full layer, which is worth knowing rather than pretending otherwise.

sections.h: Where Korean formulation genuinely helps
sections.body: Korea permits a set of modern UV filters that let formulators build light fluids and gels rather than heavy creams, and that texture advantage is not vanity when your face is already uncomfortable. The local vocabulary is useful when shopping: 무기자차 (mugijacha) for mineral filters, 유기자차 (yugijacha) for organic ones, 혼합자차 (honhapjacha) for a mix. Look for the PA rating alongside SPF for UVA coverage. Pick something you will genuinely reapply — a sunscreen abandoned by July protects nobody, regardless of the number on the tube.

sections.h: Reapplication in real life
sections.body: Sticks and cushions are the common Korean workaround for topping up over makeup, and they are a compromise rather than an equivalent: convenient, and usually applied more thinly than the layer they are topping up. Shade, a hat and long sleeves do work that no formula matches, and they cost nothing to reapply. If you are on a prescription retinoid, ask your clinician whether anything else in your plan raises sun sensitivity further, since some oral medications carry their own caution.

rx.title: Choosing a Moisturiser on Isotretinoin
rx.h1: What to look for in a moisturiser during an isotretinoin course
rx.qa: During an isotretinoin course the moisturiser people are commonly steered towards is the least interesting one available: fragrance-free, active-free, and richer than whatever they were using before. Occlusive textures matter more than clever ingredients here, and lips almost always need a plain ointment rather than a balm. Your prescriber knows what your skin is doing and should be the one consulted if dryness becomes painful or does not settle.

sections.h: Read the label for what is missing
sections.body: The useful question is not which hero ingredient a cream contains but what it has left out. Fragrance, essential oils, drying alcohols, acids, retinol and strong vitamin C are the usual things to avoid on skin behaving this way. That rules out a surprising share of the Korean shelf, because fragrance is common even in products marketed as gentle. Korean packaging carries a full 전성분 (jeonseongbun, 'full ingredient list'), so the information is there — you just have to look past the front of the box.

sections.h: Texture beats cleverness
sections.body: Skin that has become very dry generally responds better to something occlusive than to something sophisticated. Balms, ointments and heavy creams sit on the surface and slow water loss; a light gel essence evaporates and leaves you where you started. Korea's range of weights makes this easy to navigate — 크림 (keurim, cream) to 밤 (bam, balm) to sleeping packs used purely as an overnight occlusive. Applying while skin is still slightly damp after cleansing is a reliable improvement. Reapply during the day if your face is tight; there is no prize for restraint here.

sections.h: Lips, eyes, nose and everywhere else
sections.body: Lips are the near-universal complaint and a plain ointment used constantly outperforms every tinted or flavoured balm. Keep one in every bag, coat and bedside drawer, because the fix is frequency rather than product. The inside of the nose, the eyes and the body all dry out too, so an unscented body cream and a humidifier in a Korean winter do real work. Contact lens wearers often struggle. Anything painful, cracking, bleeding or affecting your vision goes to your doctor rather than into a shopping basket.

sections.h: What to leave alone entirely
sections.body: Exfoliants of every kind, cleansing brushes, sheet masks that sting, warming or tingling products, acid toners and anything marketed as resurfacing. A stinging product on this skin is not activating anything; it is telling you it does not belong. Sunscreen stays, since photosensitivity is commonly flagged during a course, and a comfortable formula matters more than a maximal one. Wait for the prescriber's word before reintroducing actives — including after the course finishes, when skin is often still not behaving as it did before.

rx.title: Cleansing While on Prescription Actives
rx.h1: Cleansing around a prescription: the step people get wrong first
rx.qa: On any prescription active, the cleanser is usually the first thing worth changing and the last thing people think about — a high-foaming, squeaky-clean wash makes a medicated routine considerably more uncomfortable than it needs to be. The general pattern is one mild low-foam or cream cleanser in the evening, water or a very light rinse in the morning, no brushes and no scrubs. How cleansing should sit around your specific medication is worth asking your prescriber.

sections.h: Squeaky is a warning, not a result
sections.body: The tight, squeaking feeling after washing is widely marketed as cleanliness and is better read as over-stripping, especially on skin already being dried by a prescription. Low-foam gels, cream cleansers, milks and balms all clean adequately; the foam is largely theatre. Lukewarm water rather than hot, a short wash rather than a lengthy massage, and patting rather than rubbing dry are the unglamorous adjustments that make the biggest difference. If your cleanser is the reason your face stings when the medication goes on, change the cleanser.

sections.h: Does double cleansing still apply?
sections.body: It applies when there is something to remove. If you wear sunscreen, makeup or a heavy sun stick, an oil or balm first genuinely helps get it off without scrubbing, and 이중세안 (ijungsean, 'double cleansing') exists for that reason rather than as a daily ritual requirement. If you wear none of those, one gentle wash is enough and two is just more disruption. The morning is where most people over-cleanse; water alone, or a very light cleanser, is a common recommendation for medicated skin.

sections.h: What to remove from the sink entirely
sections.body: Cleansing brushes, konjac sponges used vigorously, scrub cleansers with grains, 각질 (gakjil) removing gels, and cleansers built around acids while you are on a prescription active. Korean cleansers frequently contain low levels of AHA or BHA without shouting about it, so the ingredient list matters more than the marketing. Hot water and long steamy showers belong on the same list. None of this is about being precious — it is about not doing the medication's job twice on skin that only has one surface.

sections.h: Timing, and the question to ask
sections.body: Whether to apply a medication straight after washing or to let skin dry first, and whether moisturiser goes before or after, are the two questions people improvise most often. Both change how much irritation a given person gets, and both have real answers for your specific prescription — from the person who wrote it. Ask at the appointment, and ask again if the routine changes. In the meantime, keep the cleanser boring, because it is the one step you repeat every single day without thinking.

rx.title: Layering K-Beauty Around a Dermatologist's Plan
rx.h1: Building a Korean routine around a plan you did not write
rx.qa: The workable arrangement is a hierarchy: the prescription is the plan, and the Korean routine is support that must not compete with it. In practice that means cleansing, hydration, moisturising and sunscreen stay, additional actives generally go, and anything you want to add gets raised at an appointment rather than trialled quietly. Your clinician cannot advise on a routine they have not been told about, which makes disclosure the whole game.

sections.h: Decide what each product is for
sections.body: A useful exercise is to sort your shelf into four piles: cleanse, hydrate, moisturise, protect — and a fifth pile of actives. The first four are almost always compatible with a prescription, provided they are fragrance-light and gentle. The fifth is where conflicts live: acids, retinols, strong vitamin C, exfoliating pads, tingling ampoules. Most people discover the fifth pile is much bigger than they thought, because Korean products bury exfoliants inside things that look like toners and essences. Read ingredient lists, not category names.

sections.h: One variable at a time
sections.body: The reason clinicians dislike elaborate routines during treatment is not aesthetic snobbery. It is that when something flares, an eleven-product routine gives you eleven suspects and no way to narrow them. Introduce nothing new in the settling-in phase. After that, add one product, use it long enough to see how skin responds, and write down what it was and when. Dated notes sound obsessive until the day your dermatologist asks what changed and you can actually answer.

sections.h: Where Korean routines genuinely add something
sections.body: Comfort, adherence and sun protection — the three things that decide whether a prescription plan survives contact with real life. Korea's 진정 (jinjeong, 'calming') and barrier categories are deep and well made, the moisturiser range covers every weight from watery gel to ointment, and the sunscreen category is the best in the world at textures people will actually reapply. Those are not small contributions. They are just support rather than treatment, and the marketing that blurs the two is the thing to stay sceptical about.

sections.h: The things that are never yours to change
sections.body: Starting, stopping, pausing, buffering, alternating or 'saving' a prescription for a special occasion. Those are all clinical decisions, and adjusting them because a routine felt harsh last Tuesday is the most common way people lose months. If the plan is unbearable, that is a reason to go back and say so — prescribers can usually change the vehicle, the pairing or the approach. Nothing on this page substitutes for the instructions of the clinician who knows your skin.

rx.title: What 'Keep It Simple' Actually Means
rx.h1: Your dermatologist said keep it simple: here is what they meant
rx.qa: When a clinician says to keep it simple during treatment they usually mean fewer products, fewer actives, no fragrance and — crucially — nothing new, rather than 'buy a minimalist Korean set'. The instruction is about removing variables while the medication does its work, not about aesthetics or brand choice. If you are unsure whether a specific product counts as simple, the fastest route is to ask the person who said it.

sections.h: Four products, not four hundred won
sections.body: The usual shape is a gentle cleanser, a moisturiser, a sunscreen and the prescription. Sometimes a hydrating layer if skin is very dry. That is it, and it is meant to feel underwhelming. The instruction is not about price, packaging or how minimal a brand looks — a five-ingredient serum in beautiful packaging is still an extra variable. Nor does it mean throwing everything away permanently. It means putting things aside for a defined period that your clinician, not the internet, brings to an end.

sections.h: 'Nothing new' is the part people miss
sections.body: Most people successfully cut their routine down and then immediately buy a new gentle cleanser to do it with. That is still a new product on treated skin, and if a reaction follows, nobody can tell whether it was the prescription or the purchase. Simple means using what you already know your skin tolerates. If your existing cleanser is genuinely the problem, replace it deliberately, singly, and tell your clinician you have. Travel makes this harder — a Korea trip is a poor moment to start a treatment plan.

sections.h: Why the instruction exists at all
sections.body: Two reasons. Irritation compounds, so each additional active raises the chance the plan becomes unbearable and gets abandoned. And attribution collapses, so a flare in a large routine cannot be traced. Clinicians have watched this happen enough times to open with the warning. There is also a quieter reason: skincare marketing is relentless, and a stressful patch of skin is exactly when people are most susceptible to it. Simplicity is partly a defence against your own 3am shopping.

sections.h: When things come back
sections.body: Ask specifically, and ask for an order. Which product returns first, what to watch for, and what to do if it does not go well are all fair questions at a follow-up. Expect the answer to be slower than you want and singular rather than a list. Vitamin C, acids and cosmetic retinoids are the usual candidates to reintroduce last. Reintroduce one, keep everything else stable, and resist the urge to celebrate a good week by restoring your entire shelf at once.

rx.title: How to Talk to a Dermatologist About Your Routine
rx.h1: Bringing your existing Korean routine to a dermatology appointment
rx.qa: The most useful thing you can bring to a dermatology appointment is an accurate list of everything already going on your face, including the products you assume are too gentle to matter. Photographs of ingredient lists work better than brand names, especially for imported Korean products a clinician outside Korea will not recognise. Every recommendation that follows is theirs to make; your job is to make sure they are working from real information.

sections.h: Photograph the ingredient lists, not the bottles
sections.body: A brand name tells a clinician nothing if the product is Korean and they are not. The ingredient list tells them everything, and Korean packaging carries a full 전성분 (jeonseongbun, 'full ingredient list') by law. Photograph the back of each product before the appointment. Where the list is printed in Korean only, most items are still recognisable INCI names transliterated into Hangul, and a translation app plus the pictures gets you most of the way. Include cleansers, sunscreen and anything from a bathhouse or hotel.

sections.h: Declare the things that do not feel like skincare
sections.body: Supplements, oral medications from other doctors, recent salon treatments, brow threading, waxing, home devices, LED masks, dermarollers, and anything a friend gave you from an unlabelled tube. Also declare what you are planning: a peel booked next month, a Korea trip built around clinic appointments, a wedding. Clinicians make different decisions when they know a laser is coming. Omitting things because they feel embarrassing or trivial is the main way a consultation goes wrong, and nobody in that room is judging your shelf.

sections.h: Ask better questions than 'is this good?'
sections.body: Useful ones: which of these should stop, and for how long. Which can stay. What should I expect in the first stretch, and what would count as a reaction rather than an adjustment. What do I do if that happens, and how do I reach you. When do things come back, and in what order. Is there anything here that makes me more sun-sensitive. If cost or availability is a constraint, say so — substitutions are usually possible and are better decided in the room.

sections.h: If you are consulting in Korea as a visitor
sections.body: Bring your product photographs and a written list of medications with generic names rather than brand names, since brands differ by country. Ask what the follow-up arrangement is if something goes wrong after you fly home, because the honest answer is often that a doctor where you live becomes responsible. Ask for the aftercare instructions in writing. Interpretation is available at many 피부과 (pibugwa, dermatology clinics) in Seoul, and it is worth requesting rather than improvising through a phone.
